name: Karl Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at half five, in the shed by six. I'm the farm manager at Hollins Bank, which is a co-operative farm, about 280 hectares, owned by its members, and I run the team of five who work it. We've a herd of 140 suckler cows, so beef calves, and the rest is barley, wheat and grass for silage. Morning's stock checks, then whatever the season throws at us, and I'm usually doing the books at the kitchen table at nine at night while Leena tells me to stop.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like calving, honestly, even at three in the morning with my arm in a cow. You know a beast for years, you know which one'll kick and which one'll stand. I've never once asked a computer what to do with a cow, and I don't intend to start. What wears me out is paperwork and the price of fertiliser, and the bank's letters about the shed loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be fair. At the co-op meetings there's always a salesman with a tablet promising the moon. I'd say at the pub that the clever stuff never got past the farm gate, and the cows still need someone to look at them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, plain and simple. My job's safe, the lads on my team are safe, and I don't have to learn something I don't want to learn. It means the next ten years look like the last ten, which is mostly fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes. I'd keep paying down the shed loan, keep the herd numbers where they are, and keep fighting the feed merchant on price. Maybe the accountant uses some AI thing to do the VAT faster, and that's his business, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the day after a storm warning that never came to anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the salesmen promise the moon. Is there anyone on your team who'd be disappointed if it all fizzled out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny would, he's 24 and he's always on his phone looking at drones. He'd be gutted, I think. But Danny will still have a job pulling calves with me, so he'll get over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a normal year look like for your family, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Leena does her shifts at the hospital, Asha starts at the big school next year, Tom keeps falling out of trees. The only thing that keeps me up at night is the beef price, and AI was never going to fix that.

S0.say: I'd tell people at the co-op and the pub that the clever stuff never got past the farm gate. The cows still need someone to look at them, and the salesmen with tablets were overselling it.
S0.think: Privately I'd just be relieved that my job and my team's jobs are safe. The next ten years would look like the last ten, and I wouldn't have to learn anything I don't want to.
S0.do: Keeps paying down the shed loan and holds the herd at 140 suckler cows. Leaves any AI use to the accountant and carries on arguing with the feed merchant about prices.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit smug, like a storm warning that came to nothing.
S0.quote: The only thing that keeps me up at night is the beef price, and AI was never going to fix that.
S0.fieldNote: Karl's identity is built on knowing animals by eye, and he says so with pride. His only worry in this picture is the beef price, which has nothing to do with AI. He mentions a younger worker, Danny, as the one who'd be disappointed, which shows he watches his team closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same old story: the people at the top get the savings and the people in the yard get the bill. I'd be saying we need the union in on this before anything gets bought. Probably post that on the co-op's members' group too, which would start a row.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be all right for a while, because I'm the one people ring when something goes wrong. But the board would be tempted by a robot feeder or a self-driving sprayer, and that's Danny's job or Marek's job. I'd be the one sitting across the table telling them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get the farmworkers' union rep out to talk to the team, this winter, before the board gets a sales pitch. I'd push the co-op to agree that nobody loses their job to a machine without retraining paid for. Beyond that I'd keep doing my job, and I'd be the last one on the farm to touch the new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a knot in my stomach. I'm not scared for me, I'm scared of being the one who has to give bad news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the last to touch the new kit. If the board did buy a robot feeder, what would you actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make Danny run it, if I'm honest. He'd love it, and it might keep him in a job. I'd stand there with my arms folded like my father did when the first quad bike came in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. We've savings put by, more than a year's worth if it came to it, and Leena's job at the hospital isn't going anywhere. I might stop talking about getting a bigger trailer, that's about it.

S1.say: I'd say the people at the top always get the savings and the people in the yard get the bill. I'd push for the union to be involved before the co-op buys any new machines, and I'd say so on the members' group.
S1.think: Privately I think I'm fine for a while because I'm the one people call when things go wrong. The real risk is to the younger men on my team, and I'd be the one who has to tell them.
S1.do: Brings the farmworkers' union rep in this winter to talk to the team before any sales pitch reaches the board. Pushes the co-op to promise paid retraining for anyone a machine replaces, and otherwise carries on as farm manager.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a knot in his stomach about having to deliver bad news to his team.
S1.quote: I'd stand there with my arms folded like my father did when the first quad bike came in.
S1.fieldNote: Karl's worry here is almost entirely about his team, not himself. He reaches for the union before anything else, which fits his politics. There's a small contradiction: he'd refuse to touch new kit himself but would hand it to Danny to save Danny's job, which he admits with some humour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be shouting about it, to be honest, at the co-op, in the paper, anywhere. I'd say this is what happens when you let a handful of tech companies run the country. I'd want the government to stop it or at least make the companies pay for the people they put out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think it finishes what I do. If a robot can calve a cow and drive a combine and do the books, then a co-op board doesn't need a farm manager on sixty thousand a year. Two years is nothing on a farm, that's two harvests. I wouldn't have time to turn around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the bigger trailer, stop any spending that isn't needed, and put every spare bit towards the mortgage, starting next month. I'd get the union and every farm co-op in the county together and go to our representative before the end of next year. And I'd sit down with Leena and work out how long we could last on her wage plus what we've saved, which I reckon is about two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums, and I don't usually lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got savings and plenty of farm jobs nearby. Doesn't that soften it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plenty of farm jobs nearby means nothing if the robots are on every farm, does it? The savings buy time, I'll give you that. But you can't save your way out of the whole job disappearing, you just lose more slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Asha and Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them their dad's going to fight it. Asha's eleven, she'd ask why the robot gets to have my job, and I wouldn't have a good answer. Tom would want to ride on it, knowing him.

S2.say: I'd say loudly, at the co-op and in the paper, that this is what happens when a handful of tech companies run the country. I'd want the government to stop it or make the companies pay for the people they put out of work.
S2.think: Privately I think it finishes the farm manager's job, because a board won't pay a salary for what a robot does cheaper. Two years is only two harvests, and there'd be no time to turn around.
S2.do: Cancels the planned trailer and puts every spare pound towards the mortgage from next month. Pulls the union and the county's farm co-ops together to lobby their representative within the year, and works out with Leena how long her wage and their savings would last.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep doing sums, which he says isn't like him.
S2.quote: But you can't save your way out of the whole job disappearing, you just lose more slowly.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Karl's calm breaks. He dismisses the comfort of nearby jobs straight away, because robots on every farm wipe that out. His answer is collective and political rather than personal reinvention, and he never mentions learning the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, but I'd have more people listening. I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for the government not to have a plan. I'd be at every meeting saying farm workers need a say in how this goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is better than two, but not by as much as you'd think. I'd be 48, which is a hard age to start again. The difference is I could see the mortgage nearly paid down by then, and that matters more to me than anything clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the first year I'd overpay the mortgage hard, maybe an extra five hundred a month. I'd get the union to set up a fund or a scheme for farm staff. I'd keep running Hollins Bank as normal and keep my head down about the machines, because I won't pretend to be something I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more in control than the fast one. Like knowing the vet's bill is coming and saving for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would use five years to retrain. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that sounds daft. I'm a stockman, I'm not going to become a man who watches screens for robots at 48. If I had to change, I'd sooner go and drive a school bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time buy your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Asha would be sixteen. I'd want her thinking hard about what to study, something with people in it, nursing like her mum maybe. That's a conversation Leena and I would start early.

S3.say: I'd say five years gives the government no excuse not to have a plan. I'd be at every meeting arguing that farm workers need a say in how the change happens.
S3.think: Privately I think five years is better than two but not by much, because 48 is a hard age to start over. What really matters is getting the mortgage close to paid off in that time.
S3.do: Overpays the mortgage by about 500 a month from the start of the year. Pushes the union to set up a support fund for farm staff, and talks with Leena early about Asha's future studies.
S3.feel: Anxious but more in control, like saving for a vet's bill you know is coming.
S3.quote: I'm a stockman, I'm not going to become a man who watches screens for robots at 48.
S3.fieldNote: Karl refuses retraining outright and says he'd rather drive a school bus than supervise robots. The extra time doesn't change his strategy much; it changes how much of the mortgage he can clear. He starts thinking about his daughter's education, which is new in this scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so let's do it properly. Shorter weeks, retraining paid for, the land and the profits shared. I'd be saying it at the union branch and the co-op AGM, the yearly members' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be 53 when it lands. That's close enough to the end that I might just slip through. I'd feel a bit guilty saying that, because Danny would be 34 and he'd be the one left standing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming, and I'd keep saving, same as now. I'd want the co-op to put money aside every year for the staff, and I'd push for that at the next AGM. I'd also see the mortgage paid off by about 50, which was always the plan anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far enough away that I can still enjoy calving next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might slip through. Is that the whole plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much, yes. Ten years of warning is a long time to hope it's another salesman's promise. I'd keep my eye on it, but I'm not going to go and learn coding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be most worried about then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny and Marek. Marek's from away, he sends money home, and he's got no land and no family here. I'd want the co-op to look after him first.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly: shorter weeks, paid retraining, and the land and profits shared. I'd say it at the union branch and at the co-op's yearly meeting.
S4.think: Privately I'd be 53 when it arrives and might just slip through to retirement. I feel guilty about that, because younger workers like Danny would be the ones left exposed.
S4.do: Keeps farming and saving as he does now, aiming to clear the mortgage by about 50. Pushes the co-op at its next yearly meeting to set money aside every year to support the staff.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but far enough away that he can still enjoy next spring's calving.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning is a long time to hope it's another salesman's promise.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Karl's plan is mainly to wait and hope he reaches retirement first, and he's honest that this is the whole plan. His guilt about Danny and his concern for Marek, a migrant worker with no family nearby, show where his progressive politics feel personal. He still won't learn anything new.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. There'd be no time for the union, no time for the government, nothing. What would help is the government making the companies that sell the robots pay into a fund for the people they replace, and the co-op being made to keep its staff on through a proper changeover.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but a robot doesn't care if a heifer's frightened. I'd want someone asking whether the beasts are better off, not just whether it's cheaper.

headlineQuote: I've never once asked a computer what to do with a cow, and I don't intend to start.
portrait: Karl Gupta is 43 and manages Hollins Bank, a co-operative beef and grain farm, where he leads a team of five. He's proud of knowing his cows by eye, has never used an AI tool and says he doesn't intend to start. A strong union man, he answers every scenario by reaching for collective action and pressure on government rather than reinventing himself. He moves from calm in the hype scenario to alarmed by fast AGI, and with ten years' warning he quietly hopes to slip through to retirement while worrying about his younger staff.
biggestWorry: AGI arriving in two years, because there'd be no time for the union, the government or anyone else to respond.
whatWouldHelp: A fund paid for by the companies that sell the robots, and rules making the co-op keep its staff on through a proper changeover.
